full_text:
Interviewer:	The project that we're working on, we're interviewing women from all the different engineering disciplines about their decision to study engineering, their experiences of the course so far and what they're hopes are for the future. The purpose of it all is that we're looking at women's first experiences of the industry and how that impacts on their future career intentions (OK). And we're hoping to improve the retention of women, in the engineering industry. There's a lot of information out there saying more women are doing engineering but they tend to leave, after a while. So that's like the background of the project. I'll start off asking you a few background questions. Can you tell me, is it product design you're doing?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	Maths, physics and art and design…

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Erm all girls Grammar.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, well I did architecture, for – just for a placement, at school, other than that nothing.

Interviewer:	OK. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK when and why do you think that you decided to do product design then?

Subject:	Er, well when I was younger I liked all the sort of options available, it was sort of the only one that would incorporate all 3 of my A levels, and I didn't want to drop any one in particular, so it seemed liked the best option.

Interviewer:	OK, did you think about what you wanted to do career wise, when you chose your A levels?

Subject:	I had no idea, and I still don't. Not really.

Interviewer:	Did you just choose the subjects on the basis of the ones you enjoyed then?

Subject:	Yeah. Basically just because I enjoyed it and I didn't want to like throw away any one of them, so…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there's any other factors that influenced your decision to do an engineering based subject - did you have any careers advice when you were at school, anything like that?

Subject:	Er, yeah, our careers were quite good but I think they were a bit shocked when I decided to come here and do a sort of engineering – well it's quite renowned for its engineering, but I suppose a lot of the girls from my school have gone into sort of engineering or maths and that kind of field, anyway, so it wasn't really that big a surprise I think, 'cos there was the direction a lot of us go.

Interviewer:	So your school were quite supportive of doing traditionally male subjects?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, have your family been supportive?

Subject:	Yes, very. They erm…

Interviewer:	OK, did you know any engineers to talk to, or anyone that had gone into similar fields?

Subject:	Not really, no. Well my grandfather sort of did engineering, in a sense. He was sort of really quite technical minded but that was really about it.

Interviewer:	OK, What is it then, about the subject that you think does appeal to you?

Subject:	I suppose it's 'cos I have the subjects that I enjoyed at school, but that was really about it – I suppose I didn't really know an awful lot about it till I started it so it was just a fluke really, I think.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider doing any of the other types of engineering?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Not at all?

Subject:	No. I'm not a – well, as I say like the course I'm doing because it's a bit more design orientated – whereas I don't think I could cope with like the solid – full engineering, 'cos our course is sort of a mixture of the design and sort of engineering, so it's not as heavy going, I suppose.

Interviewer:	Did you look at the course – the one that is in the design technology department?

Subject:	The industrial design?

Interviewer:	The industrial design.

Subject:	I didn't actually, no.

Interviewer:	OK. How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

Subject:	Erm, probably because of its reputation mainly and because I'm not actually from England it was just a matter of almost picking from a hat really, what courses did the sort of subjects that I liked and then, you know, what universities did those at (mock?) courses, so it wasn't really a – well not like planned.

Interviewer:	Did you know, when you started uni, that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	And what do you think are the advantages of doing that?

Subject:	Basically just getting experience, because everywhere they all – everybody just wants experience and if you don't have it then you know, it's a bit difficult to get a bit further, so I think that was the main reason. 

Interviewer:	OK When you started your course, did you realise that engineering was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, I knew it was – I knew it was fairly male dominated but I didn't think it was going to be as male dominated as it is, because I think there's only 3 girls on my course

Interviewer:	Out of how many?

Subject:	Out of about 50 something (really?) So it was a bit of a shock yeah.

Interviewer:	Did it ever bother you at all?

Subject:	Erm, I think a little bit, just to begin with, just at the getting to know everybody and like, just getting to know what the guys are like, as to whether they were gonna sort of like be, oh you're a girl kind of thing. But they're all really good so it doesn't bother me now, 'cos at least they see me as somebody else, they don't see you as a girl as such, so that's quite good.

Interviewer:	Do you think it might have been more of a shock, coming from a girls' school?

Subject:	Yes, definitely.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah. I think girls still think it's sort of – you know you're gonna be considered to be odd if you like those sort of subjects or you know, you're sort of cliqueish and that kind of thing, so – yeah, but it's not like that any more so..

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done to encourage more women, do you think it's about education, about what engineering actually is?

Subject:	Yeah, I think and – I think 'cos a lot of teachers – well, I know from my school, a lot of teachers are still sort of from the older generation so they still thought of it being very male, so I think at least it's worth educating staff and teachers in schools as to like how it's changed so much and that it's so – how broad it is as well into the fact that, you know, girls could do it as well.

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer or a good product designer?

Subject:	I suppose technical minded in a sense, organised and …

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of the characteristics that make a good product designer are more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose a lot of people would say that the design would be more female, but the manufacturing side would be more male. But erm I don't know about that really.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	What?

Subject:	I suppose you get a lot of help, so if you don't – if you can't do something and you're not strong enough to do something then there's always plenty of people willing to help, so that's quite good. So I think just the help you get, although some people can kind of think oh you are a girl, you shouldn't be doing this so – but that's about it really.

Interviewer:	OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	No, it's a lot more – they sort of – I got the impression, from the prospectus, it was going to be a lot more design, but there's a lot more manufacture, which is – well is a shock, but I enjoy it, so it's OK.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Oh, erm, the worst probably is some of the – well some of the modules that I have to do, I don't quite see the relevance of them, so that – I don't really enjoy them though, I suppose. And the best is probably – I dunno, apart from the people.

Interviewer:	When you say that you don't see the relevance of some of the modules, do you mean as in you don't think that you'll use them when you leave?

Subject:	Yeah, it's more like the integrated studies kind of modules, in that you're doing things that you're only doing for maybe a few weeks, and you're not actually being – you haven't actually done any lectures on them. So you don't have enough knowledge to fully understand what you're doing, and it's not carried on so you don't – you don't feel you get anything from it.

Interviewer:	Are you pleased then that you did choose this course?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	One.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the female lecturers have the same sort of style of teaching?

Subject:	Not really. I don't think they have sort of the same sort of I suppose control, in a sense, because it is – there are so many males. It's sort of like – they can sort of get away with it. I suppose she – she's not actually teaching us for engineering but she teaches us for maths, so that's different – she's probably not as loud and sort of sit down and keep quiet kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers do you think?

Subject:	Er, I don't know if they had the confidence and they were sort of strong enough to stand up in front of everybody and make them sort of behave and just get on with it then yeah, but I think that the male teaching lecturers are really good anyway, so it doesn't really make a lot of difference.. It – probably it would be nice to see, you know, more women in you know – people that are in engineering but I don't know.

Interviewer:	Yes, OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female students the same as the male students?

Subject:	Er, the majority of them do, yeah. The odd one or two, either exclude you or not really consider you as part of the group, or will pick on you one or the other.

Interviewer:	How do you deal with that when that happens? Does it bother you?

Subject:	Er, it doesn't really bother me, you just – I suppose you just get on with it. If they do that, a lot of the blokes in the group will sort of stick up for you in a sense, because they can see that it's not right. Er, it's not too bad.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with them – are they approachable?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	Erm, again really it doesn't really bother me. He's really approachable and he's a nice man, so I'm quite happy.

Interviewer:	OK, has there been anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course? There might not have been…

Subject:	Not really.

Interviewer:	OK have you had to do much group work?

Subject:	Yes, lots.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Yeah. If everybody pulls their weight, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you do group work, do you get to choose who you want to work with or do you get put in groups?

Subject:	Most of the time we get put into groups.

Interviewer:	OK, and do you get the chance to work with the other girls on the course very often?

Subject:	Not really, not unless we pick groups and that's not very often.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that women are easier to work with in groups? Do you think it makes any difference?

Subject:	Erm, working with other women, I'd probably say no, because I'd say quite a lot of us are quite stubborn in a sense, whereas if you're working with other men, then it's easier because well I suppose you can sort of, well not bully them in a sense but sort of sweet talk them round a little bit, but I think it's harder working with other girls.

Interviewer:	OK, is it fair to say that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah. I think girls tend to be a lot more organised than the guys they sort of leave everything til' the last minute and are a bit rushed, whereas the girls sort of like to organise them all.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Yes, bad ones have probably been – well we're working in a group at the minute actually that's not particularly enjoyable because – well one of the guys is – I feel that he has the impression that you're just a girl, which I find quite annoying, so we don't really see eye to eye on a lot of things and I find him quite sort of domineering, that he's just came and took the role of leader – it's sort of like you will do this, this, and this. And there's no sort of leverage for different opinions in the group so, that's been a bit of a battle.

Interviewer:	How do you try and deal with that situation?

Subject:	It's very difficult – it's difficult because he is – I find that our – just in general, our personalities clash. So, trying to like even sit down and tell him that I don't want to do something or that I think somebody else should do something different but it's – it's quite difficult but I suppose trying to get the whole group together and discuss it as a group, rather than him just sort of dictating to everybody, but …

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the benefits of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, more opinions on what's actually happening. Erm, I suppose more heads are better than one, that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it will have benefits, when you go to work as well? The experience of doing group work?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah because nothing you do - you don't do anything on your own.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel that there are any aspects of teaching or advice that you've had that will help you on your placement?

Subject:	I don't know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you'll use the technical skills that you've learnt?

Subject:	Erm, I hope so. I suppose it depends what kind of placement I get at the end. But I suppose the skills like being organised and being able to work in groups and just getting on with work on your own – that kind of thing will definitely help

Interviewer:	Do you think that the week experience that you had, when you were at school, do you think that will help you at all when you go?

Subject:	No. I hated it so …

Interviewer:	OK, that's fair enough. Do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement now?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so.

Interviewer:	Has the university been much help in preparing you for the placement in industry?

Subject:	Oh, I don't know, they've given us a lot of help in trying to find a placement but I don't say - that's probably about it

Interviewer:	Have they given you any idea of what to expect when you're on the placement?

Subject:	No, not really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that they should do?

Subject:	Erm, I think – a little bit maybe but I think at the same time, it should be up to us to actually speak to people who've been on placements. I mean whether the university should actually bring in people who've been on placements and get them to talk to us, or leave it up to us – but we should sort of be speaking to those people.

Interviewer:	Have you spoken to the people that have been on placement?

Subject:	Er, 1 or 2 but not very many really – just people who have – that have been to interviews, and I've had a chance to speak to the people already there, like (?)

Interviewer:	Did you find that useful?

Subject:	Yeah. I would say it was enlightening.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the whole educational experience, and the way that you're taught reflects at all what it's going to be like when you're in industry?

Subject:	Erm, probably not. 

Interviewer:	What do you think will be different?

Subject:	Erm, dunno – I think – but I suppose here at least if you don't do your work, you're given a kick, but in industry if you don't do it, you're probably gonna end up with the sack so it's slightly different. More 

Interviewer:	More responsibility?

Subject:	Yeah, you sort of – I suppose part of the team, that if you don't do something then it could lead to company failure or something like that, so yeah.

Interviewer:	You may have already started to say about this, but why is it that you really want to go on placement? What do you think you'll gain from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, it's just the experience in that you can go to – maybe working on a project, you can say well I do have this behind me. I haven't like just come straight from university, I've actually been out there and worked for a while so, I think that'll help.

Interviewer:	Do you think it'll help you make your mind up what you want to do, more long-term as well?

Subject:	Hopefully – yeah. It'll tell me whether I absolutely hate engineering or love it, hopefully.

Interviewer:	OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, my parents probably – they really encouraged me. I don't think anybody's discouraged me, really much. Erm, probably some of the employers have discouraged me, in the sense that they've been quite uncooperative or rude, in a sense.

Interviewer:	Is that when you've been to interviews or (?)

Subject:	Not too much interviews, but when I've been applying in that it's like I've been waiting to hear from one for about 4 weeks now, and I was told that I would hear, like 4 weeks ago and I felt encouraged and so – and when I call them, my calls just get re-directed and stuff, so I think that's quite rude. So that's kind of put me off a little bit – things like that but I think my parents have encouraged me quite a bit and like I'd say the staff have been encouraging quite a bit they say, like keep trying.

Interviewer:	OK, did you say you don't know where you're going yet?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, what have you been looking for in a company and what has attracted you to the companies that you have applied for?

Subject:	Erm, probably more – a bit more of the design aspect rather than full on engineering, but a mixture of both – companies that will actually do the design work and then carry out right the way through. So that kind of thing rather than just going into solid engineering or something.

Interviewer:	Have you looked at other things like pay or training opportunities and career prospects, or location – have you looked at anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, location mainly – has been probably the strongest one, because initially I wanted to stay fairly local to here, but that's changed now and I'm sort of looking wider for something because I'm not finding anything. Erm, pay – a little bit but it's probably not as much as erm other things like where it actually is and what it does.

Interviewer:	OK what about the opportunities for a job with the company, when you've maybe finished?

Subject:	Erm, if it's there then that'd be nice but I'm not really too bothered.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. What sort of research have you done into the companies that you've applied to?

Subject:	Erm, like looking at their web sites and I go to the careers services and try to find out their profiles and find out if anybody else has been there for jobs there before. That kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Is the careers service here quite helpful?

Subject:	Yeah. I haven't really spoken to anybody in there as such but like I've been able to find things I've been looking for so…

Interviewer:	Ok, you said that the university have been quite helpful in helping you find placements – what sort of help or advice have they given you?

Subject:	Er just around things like opportunities – they've like, every week, we probably get 3 or 4 emails like saying that there's a placement going for such and such and like what qualifications you need for it and things like that. And – and they've had, well we've meetings coming up to see who exactly has got placements and where everybody else stands as to their placements, and arrange times that we can go to the careers service to ask for help or to do practice interviews and things like that, so. I think that's been quite good.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you happy with all that? Is there anything else that you'd like to see them do?

Subject:	Erm, not really, I think that's – I think that's quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, what sorts of things are you hoping to get out of your placement?

Subject:	Erm, confidence and the ability to like work for a company and to not have it all go wrong hopefully.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that you'll be able to use what you've learnt, on your placement, in your final year, the same as you hope to use what you've done so far, when you're on placement?

Subject:	Yeah. I should hope I'll be more organised in the old like manage my time better and my work better, and that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the worst and best things about being on placement or what are you most looking forward to or worried about?

Subject:	Erm, I'm probably most worried about whether I'll enjoy it or not. Best thing probably be meeting new people, and new experiences and actually doing the job. Erm, and probably the worst thing will be missing friends.

Interviewer:	OK, when you're actually on your placement, do you know how much support or connection you'll still have with the university?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I know we still have – we're all assigned tutors who will come visit us and things like that and that are there for us to email if there's problems and that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you find that reassuring?

Subject:	Yeah, probably – you know you're not going to lose contact with the university, that if everything goes completely wrong then you're not gonna be stuck in something that you really hate.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, in terms of your career then, what do you think you'll be doing in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Oh I have no idea – really no idea. Erm, hopefully something that I enjoy and that will use what I'm actually learning at the minute 'cos I don't think I'd like to just throw it all away and do something completely different.

Interviewer:	So what would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	I'd probably really like to work for some sort of consultancy – engineering design consultancy that type of thing.

Interviewer:	What is it that appeals to you about doing that?

Subject:	Erm, probably the same as what I'm looking for in a placement – they do their own sort of designs, and they work with sort of big companies and it – you see it through to manufacture but it's not just only the engineering of one thing.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I think so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that they're good for getting in, in the first place and to climb up the career ladder once you're in?

Subject:	I think probably getting into it, is probably a little more difficult because there doesn't seem to be that many opportunities at the minute, and there's probably more and more people starting to look at these things so I suppose there's more people coming out than there are jobs available so – and you know that probably you're gonna have to compete against people who've done a more streamlined form of engineering, which could be more difficult.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more long-term you'd like to go into management within the field that you're in?

Subject:	Yeah, probably because I'm doing a management module at the minute, which I've really enjoyed so possibly.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far?

Subject:	So far yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	I don't think so.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Erm, intelligent, motivated and creative and …

Interviewer:	Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Not really – it probably wouldn't have been one I would have thought of – I suppose it is, but it's not what would spring to mind.

Interviewer:	Do you think that people think that it is masculine – is that just because of the numbers of males in the industry (yeah probably) as well as to do with the type of work as well?

Subject:	Probably a bit of both in as much as I suppose a lot of people will see engineering as quite heavy work and sort of that males are more technical minded than women and women can be a bit silly and that kind of thing, be a bit – but I think with education now it's sort of changing a bit, like girls are realising they can do a lot more with their life.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will improve for women in the industry then?

Subject:	Er, I don't know to be honest, I think it'll probably stay this way for a good wee while. I think a lot of women are like a lot of schools and stuff, put women off – and then maybe just coming from an all girls school you didn't have the male influence, so you felt you could do anything, whereas if you're coming from a mixed school, you are around males all the time. So you might think doing an engineering degree, they'll think I'm strange or you know, I'll get bullied and things like that – I think that probably makes a difference.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact that it is so male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	Erm, possibly career wise, if – if you end up in a company where it's still male dominated and they don't have a very open-minded view of women coming into the company, but at the same time I suppose if you get the job, then they have to have a degree of willingness, to let women in. So I think it will probably be – there's one or two people, in the main company, that are sort of cynical, so.

Interviewer:	Does that worry you at all?

Subject:	Erm, not really because I think you'd find that anywhere be it management or sort of technology or something like that.

Interviewer:	Yeah – OK that's everything thank you very much – that was very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know, when you started uni, that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what do you think are the advantages of doing that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Basically just getting experience, because everywhere they all – everybody just wants experience and if you don't have it then you know, it's a bit difficult to get a bit further, so I think that was the main reason.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK When you started your course, did you realise that engineering was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I knew it was – I knew it was fairly male dominated but I didn't think it was going to be as male dominated as it is, because I think there's only 3 girls on my course

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Out of how many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Out of about 50 something (really?) So it was a bit of a shock yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it ever bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think a little bit, just to begin with, just at the getting to know everybody and like, just getting to know what the guys are like, as to whether they were gonna sort of like be, oh you're a girl kind of thing. But they're all really good so it doesn't bother me now, 'cos at least they see me as somebody else, they don't see you as a girl as such, so that's quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it might have been more of a shock, coming from a girls' school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I think girls still think it's sort of – you know you're gonna be considered to be odd if you like those sort of subjects or you know, you're sort of cliqueish and that kind of thing, so – yeah, but it's not like that any more so..

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be done to encourage more women, do you think it's about education, about what engineering actually is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think and – I think 'cos a lot of teachers – well, I know from my school, a lot of teachers are still sort of from the older generation so they still thought of it being very male, so I think at least it's worth educating staff and teachers in schools as to like how it's changed so much and that it's so – how broad it is as well into the fact that, you know, girls could do it as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer or a good product designer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose technical minded in a sense, organised and …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of the characteristics that make a good product designer are more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose a lot of people would say that the design would be more female, but the manufacturing side would be more male. But erm I don't know about that really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose you get a lot of help, so if you don't – if you can't do something and you're not strong enough to do something then there's always plenty of people willing to help, so that's quite good. So I think just the help you get, although some people can kind of think oh you are a girl, you shouldn't be doing this so – but that's about it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it's a lot more – they sort of – I got the impression, from the prospectus, it was going to be a lot more design, but there's a lot more manufacture, which is – well is a shock, but I enjoy it, so it's OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, erm, the worst probably is some of the – well some of the modules that I have to do, I don't quite see the relevance of them, so that – I don't really enjoy them though, I suppose. And the best is probably – I dunno, apart from the people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you say that you don't see the relevance of some of the modules, do you mean as in you don't think that you'll use them when you leave?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it's more like the integrated studies kind of modules, in that you're doing things that you're only doing for maybe a few weeks, and you're not actually being – you haven't actually done any lectures on them. So you don't have enough knowledge to fully understand what you're doing, and it's not carried on so you don't – you don't feel you get anything from it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you pleased then that you did choose this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the female lecturers have the same sort of style of teaching?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I don't think they have sort of the same sort of I suppose control, in a sense, because it is – there are so many males. It's sort of like – they can sort of get away with it. I suppose she – she's not actually teaching us for engineering but she teaches us for maths, so that's different – she's probably not as loud and sort of sit down and keep quiet kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don't know if they had the confidence and they were sort of strong enough to stand up in front of everybody and make them sort of behave and just get on with it then yeah, but I think that the male teaching lecturers are really good anyway, so it doesn't really make a lot of difference.. It – probably it would be nice to see, you know, more women in you know – people that are in engineering but I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female students the same as the male students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the majority of them do, yeah. The odd one or two, either exclude you or not really consider you as part of the group, or will pick on you one or the other.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you deal with that when that happens? Does it bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it doesn't really bother me, you just – I suppose you just get on with it. If they do that, a lot of the blokes in the group will sort of stick up for you in a sense, because they can see that it's not right. Er, it's not too bad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with them – are they approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, again really it doesn't really bother me. He's really approachable and he's a nice man, so I'm quite happy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has there been anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course? There might not have been…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have you had to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, lots.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. If everybody pulls their weight, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you do group work, do you get to choose who you want to work with or do you get put in groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Most of the time we get put into groups.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and do you get the chance to work with the other girls on the course very often?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, not unless we pick groups and that's not very often.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that women are easier to work with in groups? Do you think it makes any difference?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, working with other women, I'd probably say no, because I'd say quite a lot of us are quite stubborn in a sense, whereas if you're working with other men, then it's easier because well I suppose you can sort of, well not bully them in a sense but sort of sweet talk them round a little bit, but I think it's harder working with other girls.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is it fair to say that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I think girls tend to be a lot more organised than the guys they sort of leave everything til' the last minute and are a bit rushed, whereas the girls sort of like to organise them all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, bad ones have probably been – well we're working in a group at the minute actually that's not particularly enjoyable because – well one of the guys is – I feel that he has the impression that you're just a girl, which I find quite annoying, so we don't really see eye to eye on a lot of things and I find him quite sort of domineering, that he's just came and took the role of leader – it's sort of like you will do this, this, and this. And there's no sort of leverage for different opinions in the group so, that's been a bit of a battle.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you try and deal with that situation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's very difficult – it's difficult because he is – I find that our – just in general, our personalities clash. So, trying to like even sit down and tell him that I don't want to do something or that I think somebody else should do something different but it's – it's quite difficult but I suppose trying to get the whole group together and discuss it as a group, rather than him just sort of dictating to everybody, but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the benefits of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, more opinions on what's actually happening. Erm, I suppose more heads are better than one, that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it will have benefits, when you go to work as well? The experience of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah because nothing you do - you don't do anything on your own.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel that there are any aspects of teaching or advice that you've had that will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you'll use the technical skills that you've learnt?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I hope so. I suppose it depends what kind of placement I get at the end. But I suppose the skills like being organised and being able to work in groups and just getting on with work on your own – that kind of thing will definitely help

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the week experience that you had, when you were at school, do you think that will help you at all when you go?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I hated it so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fair enough. Do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the university been much help in preparing you for the placement in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, I don't know, they've given us a lot of help in trying to find a placement but I don't say - that's probably about it

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have they given you any idea of what to expect when you're on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that they should do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think – a little bit maybe but I think at the same time, it should be up to us to actually speak to people who've been on placements. I mean whether the university should actually bring in people who've been on placements and get them to talk to us, or leave it up to us – but we should sort of be speaking to those people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you spoken to the people that have been on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, 1 or 2 but not very many really – just people who have – that have been to interviews, and I've had a chance to speak to the people already there, like (?)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you find that useful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I would say it was enlightening.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the whole educational experience, and the way that you're taught reflects at all what it's going to be like when you're in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, dunno – I think – but I suppose here at least if you don't do your work, you're given a kick, but in industry if you don't do it, you're probably gonna end up with the sack so it's slightly different. More

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: More responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, you sort of – I suppose part of the team, that if you don't do something then it could lead to company failure or something like that, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You may have already started to say about this, but why is it that you really want to go on placement? What do you think you'll gain from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it's just the experience in that you can go to – maybe working on a project, you can say well I do have this behind me. I haven't like just come straight from university, I've actually been out there and worked for a while so, I think that'll help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it'll help you make your mind up what you want to do, more long-term as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully – yeah. It'll tell me whether I absolutely hate engineering or love it, hopefully.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, my parents probably – they really encouraged me. I don't think anybody's discouraged me, really much. Erm, probably some of the employers have discouraged me, in the sense that they've been quite uncooperative or rude, in a sense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that when you've been to interviews or (?)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not too much interviews, but when I've been applying in that it's like I've been waiting to hear from one for about 4 weeks now, and I was told that I would hear, like 4 weeks ago and I felt encouraged and so – and when I call them, my calls just get re-directed and stuff, so I think that's quite rude. So that's kind of put me off a little bit – things like that but I think my parents have encouraged me quite a bit and like I'd say the staff have been encouraging quite a bit they say, like keep trying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you say you don't know where you're going yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what have you been looking for in a company and what has attracted you to the companies that you have applied for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably more – a bit more of the design aspect rather than full on engineering, but a mixture of both – companies that will actually do the design work and then carry out right the way through. So that kind of thing rather than just going into solid engineering or something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you looked at other things like pay or training opportunities and career prospects, or location – have you looked at anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, location mainly – has been probably the strongest one, because initially I wanted to stay fairly local to here, but that's changed now and I'm sort of looking wider for something because I'm not finding anything. Erm, pay – a little bit but it's probably not as much as erm other things like where it actually is and what it does.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what about the opportunities for a job with the company, when you've maybe finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, if it's there then that'd be nice but I'm not really too bothered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. What sort of research have you done into the companies that you've applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, like looking at their web sites and I go to the careers services and try to find out their profiles and find out if anybody else has been there for jobs there before. That kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is the careers service here quite helpful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I haven't really spoken to anybody in there as such but like I've been able to find things I've been looking for so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, you said that the university have been quite helpful in helping you find placements – what sort of help or advice have they given you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er just around things like opportunities – they've like, every week, we probably get 3 or 4 emails like saying that there's a placement going for such and such and like what qualifications you need for it and things like that. And – and they've had, well we've meetings coming up to see who exactly has got placements and where everybody else stands as to their placements, and arrange times that we can go to the careers service to ask for help or to do practice interviews and things like that, so. I think that's been quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you happy with all that? Is there anything else that you'd like to see them do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really, I think that's – I think that's quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sorts of things are you hoping to get out of your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, confidence and the ability to like work for a company and to not have it all go wrong hopefully.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that you'll be able to use what you've learnt, on your placement, in your final year, the same as you hope to use what you've done so far, when you're on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I should hope I'll be more organised in the old like manage my time better and my work better, and that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the worst and best things about being on placement or what are you most looking forward to or worried about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm probably most worried about whether I'll enjoy it or not. Best thing probably be meeting new people, and new experiences and actually doing the job. Erm, and probably the worst thing will be missing friends.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you're actually on your placement, do you know how much support or connection you'll still have with the university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I know we still have – we're all assigned tutors who will come visit us and things like that and that are there for us to email if there's problems and that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that reassuring?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, probably – you know you're not going to lose contact with the university, that if everything goes completely wrong then you're not gonna be stuck in something that you really hate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, in terms of your career then, what do you think you'll be doing in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I have no idea – really no idea. Erm, hopefully something that I enjoy and that will use what I'm actually learning at the minute 'cos I don't think I'd like to just throw it all away and do something completely different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd probably really like to work for some sort of consultancy – engineering design consultancy that type of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is it that appeals to you about doing that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably the same as what I'm looking for in a placement – they do their own sort of designs, and they work with sort of big companies and it – you see it through to manufacture but it's not just only the engineering of one thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that they're good for getting in, in the first place and to climb up the career ladder once you're in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think probably getting into it, is probably a little more difficult because there doesn't seem to be that many opportunities at the minute, and there's probably more and more people starting to look at these things so I suppose there's more people coming out than there are jobs available so – and you know that probably you're gonna have to compete against people who've done a more streamlined form of engineering, which could be more difficult.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more long-term you'd like to go into management within the field that you're in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, probably because I'm doing a management module at the minute, which I've really enjoyed so possibly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So far yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, intelligent, motivated and creative and …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really – it probably wouldn't have been one I would have thought of – I suppose it is, but it's not what would spring to mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that people think that it is masculine – is that just because of the numbers of males in the industry (yeah probably) as well as to do with the type of work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably a bit of both in as much as I suppose a lot of people will see engineering as quite heavy work and sort of that males are more technical minded than women and women can be a bit silly and that kind of thing, be a bit – but I think with education now it's sort of changing a bit, like girls are realising they can do a lot more with their life.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will improve for women in the industry then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don't know to be honest, I think it'll probably stay this way for a good wee while. I think a lot of women are like a lot of schools and stuff, put women off – and then maybe just coming from an all girls school you didn't have the male influence, so you felt you could do anything, whereas if you're coming from a mixed school, you are around males all the time. So you might think doing an engineering degree, they'll think I'm strange or you know, I'll get bullied and things like that – I think that probably makes a difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the fact that it is so male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, possibly career wise, if – if you end up in a company where it's still male dominated and they don't have a very open-minded view of women coming into the company, but at the same time I suppose if you get the job, then they have to have a degree of willingness, to let women in. So I think it will probably be – there's one or two people, in the main company, that are sort of cynical, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that worry you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really because I think you'd find that anywhere be it management or sort of technology or something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – OK that's everything thank you very much – that was very helpful.
